title: Women in Church Leadership
lead: May women preach, lead congregations or be ordained? The Bible tells of women prophets, judges and coworkers of Paul, and it also has Paul's instructions limiting women's teaching. Churches read these texts in different ways and reach different practices.

sections.h: Women who led in the Bible
sections.b: Miriam is called a prophet and leads Israel in song (Exodus 15:20–21; Micah 6:4). "Deborah, a woman and a prophet, the wife of Lappidoth, was the one judging Israel at that time" (Judges 4:4). King Josiah's officials went to Huldah, "a woman prophet," to learn God's word about the scroll found in the temple (2 Kings 22:14). Joel foresaw sons and daughters prophesying, and Peter said this came true at Pentecost (Joel 2:28–29; Acts 2:17–18). Women were the first witnesses of the resurrection (Luke 24:1–10; John 20:17–18). Paul names Phoebe a deacon or servant of the church (Romans 16:1–2), greets Junia as notable among the apostles (Romans 16:7), and mentions women who pray and prophesy in worship (1 Corinthians 11:5). Priscilla and her husband taught Apollos (Acts 18:26).

sections.b: Paul tells the Corinthians that women should keep silent in the churches (1 Corinthians 14:34–35). In 1 Timothy he says he does not permit a woman to teach or to have authority over a man, and he gives the order of creation, Adam first and then Eve, as a reason (1 Timothy 2:11–14; Genesis 2:18–23). The lists of qualities for overseers and elders describe them as the husband of one wife (1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6). Readers argue over how these fit with the women leaders above and with Paul's statement that in Christ there is "neither male nor female" (Galatians 3:28). Some say the limits are for all times; others say they answered local problems, such as false teaching at Ephesus. Scholars also debate the translation of Junia's title and of Phoebe's role.
sections.refs: 1 Corinthians 14:34–35; 1 Timothy 2:11–14; Genesis 2:18–23; 1 Timothy 3:2; Titus 1:6; Galatians 3:28

sections.b: Catholic and Orthodox churches ordain only men as priests and bishops; Pope John Paul II declared in 1994 that the church has no authority to ordain women priests. Women serve these churches in many other ways, and the Orthodox have revived women deacons in a few places. Many Baptist, Reformed and conservative Lutheran churches hold a view called complementarianism: men and women are equal in worth, but the office of pastor is for qualified men. Other churches, often called egalitarian, ordain women: most Methodist bodies, many Lutheran, Anglican and Reformed churches, the Assemblies of God and other Pentecostal churches, and the Quakers, who have recognized women's preaching since the 1600s. Both sides appeal to Scripture, not only to culture.

common: Christians agree that women and men are equally made in God's image and equally saved in Christ.
uncommon: Some hold that women may preach and teach but not serve as senior pastor or elder.
